sections.h2: Who sends and collects the tax bill
sections.html:
A single Nash County office both sets values and takes payment. Staff there list real and personal property, assess it, and collect what is owed. Visit 120 W. Washington St., Suite 2058, Nashville, NC 27856. The phone is 252-459-9824, answered through the business day from eight until five.

Relief applications under state law go through this office too. Payments go to the collector. Anything about listing, billing or an assessed value is for the assessor's staff.

Commissioners fix the rate in spring, no later than June 30. The bill is that rate times every $100 of taxable value. Statements are mailed in July or August, and a missing one by September 15 is a reason to call the collector.

sections.h2: Nash County housing at a glance
sections.html:
Roughly 99,365 people lived in Nash County in mid-2025, 4.6% more than in 2020. A middle-of-the-market owner-occupied house is worth $191,000, and 63.6% of households own. Rent typically runs $953 monthly across 45,068 housing units.

With about a third of households renting, many local houses are landlord-owned. If that is you, the county still bills the January 1 titleholder no matter what the tenant pays.

Taxes come due September 1 and stay interest-free until January 5. A weekend January 5 pushes the cutoff to the next working day. Mail postmarked by then counts, though the county urges sending it a week ahead.

On real estate and personal property, 2% interest is added for January and 0.75% for every month after that, under G.S. 105-360. Registered vehicles follow their own rule: 5% in the first month past due.

  • Between March 1 and June 30 the county may run delinquent real estate in the newspaper and bill the owner for the ad.
  • Enforcement can mean garnished wages, attached bank accounts or rents, foreclosure, or a hold on your state income tax refund.
  • You may prepay toward a bill that has not been issued; ask staff how.

Selling does not cancel the year's bill for you. Liability rests on the January 1 titleholder, and a later sale leaves it in place.

Closings usually prorate the tax, but ask your agent or attorney to confirm. To be sure, have a check made out to the Tax Collector's Office at the table. When this year's bill is not yet due, the collector accepts a prepayment figured at last year's rate.

Under G.S. 105-355, the tax lien attaches to the parcel on the listing date, and no buyer or lender will accept title with it open. When a closing date is set, get the payoff amount from the tax office in writing and hand it to the closing attorney.

A cash sale skips the lender's underwriting and escrow steps, but the tax still has to be paid from proceeds or prorated.

Start informally. Only a failed informal appeal moves on to the county review board, and nobody may skip ahead, as the county's revaluation page spells out.

There are four ways to open the informal step.

  • By appointment, face to face with an appraiser at the West Washington Street office in Nashville.
  • Over the phone, once an appraiser agrees to call you back.
  • By mail: fill in the bottom of the appeal notice and send it with your documents to the Tax Office, marked for the Board of Equalization and Review.
  • Online, using the county's informal appeal form.

Once you get the informal answer, the formal route opens for thirty days from the notice date, and the burden is on you to show the value is wrong. Under G.S. 105-322 the board's opening session falls in a spring window, April into early May.

Fairness and accuracy of the value are the only questions before the board; ability to pay is not. Your best exhibit is a set of similar nearby homes assessed lower. A board denial can be taken to the Property Tax Commission, with written notice due one month after the ruling goes out (G.S. 105-290).

Four programs exist here: an exclusion for the elderly and permanently disabled, a disabled veteran exclusion, the circuit breaker deferment, and a builder's inventory exclusion. Call (252) 459-1222 for an application, or download one from the tax forms page.

The 2026 income cap is $38,800 for the elderly or disabled exclusion and the circuit breaker, and $58,200 for the higher circuit breaker tier. The elderly or disabled exclusion removes $25,000 or half the appraised value, whichever is greater, (G.S. 105-277.1). A disabled veteran can exclude $45,000 of value regardless of age or income.

Reappraisals can be no more than eight years apart under state law, each taking effect January 1 of its scheduled year (G.S. 105-286). Nash County says the goal is a fair and accurate value on every parcel.

The project covers more than 53,000 parcels, with an outside firm, Piner Appraisal, doing the work. Its appraisers also hear informal appeals. Owners are mailed the new value, and the thirty-day clock starts on that notice date.

Nash County treats market value as a price a willing buyer and seller reach with no pressure, which rules out foreclosure and family sales. If your own sale was one of those, bring different comparables.

sections.h2: Getting ready to list a Nash County house
sections.html:
Before the sign goes up, do three things in order. First, ask the Tax Collector's Office what is owed on the parcel so no surprise appears at the closing table. Second, look at your latest assessment notice and decide whether the value could hurt a buyer's appraisal; if so, the informal appeal costs nothing but a phone call. Third, tell your closing attorney which of your exemptions or deferments are in place, since those can change what is owed.

Bring the parcel number, a photo ID and any assessment notice when you visit the office on West Washington Street. A buyer paying cash will often ask for the tax payoff within days of an offer, so having it in hand keeps the sale moving.

sections.h2: Other items the tax office handles
sections.html:
The collector also serves vehicle owners, businesses and utility customers, handy if you are closing out a household or a rental.

  • Registered motor vehicle bills are sent monthly rather than in the fall, with a separate interest rule.
  • Business licenses are issued through the Tax Collector's Office.
  • Listing forms for personal and business property are due at the office by the end of January, or a 10% penalty applies.
  • County water and sewer bills can be paid by check or cash at the Tax Collections Office in the Nashville administrative building during regular hours.

The Register of Deeds is in that building too, third floor, so one trip can cover recording a deed and asking about a payoff.

faqs.q: What is the Nash County due date?
faqs.a: Payment opens September 1 and stays penalty-free to January 5, or the next working day if that is a weekend. After that, 2% interest hits for January and 0.75% for each further month.

faqs.q: If I sell partway through the year, do I still owe that year's tax?
faqs.a: Yes, unless closing settles it. Liability follows the January 1 titleholder. Most closings prorate, and you can also pay the Tax Collector directly at the table.

faqs.q: How can I challenge my Nash County assessment?
faqs.a: Ask for an informal review by phone, mail, web form or visit. If you disagree with the result, you have thirty days from its date to file with the Board of Equalization and Review.

faqs.q: When must Nash County relief applications arrive?
faqs.a: Applications for the elderly or disabled, disabled veteran, circuit breaker and builders' inventory programs are due June 1. Form AV-10 exemptions for classified parcels are due January 31.

faqs.q: How steep is the Nash County late listing penalty?
faqs.a: Ten percent of the tax. Business and personal property listings are due by January 31, and anything later is charged the penalty.
